div.head: Introduction
div.p: The problem of scheduling real-time periodic tasks has been studied extensively [14, 12, 13, 11, 3, 91. Due to the ease of implementation and some other merits of the fixed-priority scheduling scheme [9], the timing analysis of fixed-priority scheduling algorithms has drawn considerable attention during the past decade [9]. In this paper, we study the schedulability analysis for real-time fixed-priority scheduling algorithms and propose a new, better schedulability test that can be done in polynomial time for a set of arbitrary tasks scheduled by any fixed-priority scheduling algorithm.

We consider a set of n real-time periodic tasks 7 = { T ~, 7-2,. . . , T ~} . Each task T; has a worst-case computation time C; and must be executed once every T; time units, where Ti is called the period of ri. Each invocation/execution of a periodic task is called a job. The j-th job ~; j of the i-th task ~i is ready for execution at time rij = q5i $. ( j -1) . Ti, and must be completed before time dij = 4; + ( j -1) . Moreover, we assume that tasks (jobs) are preemptable, i.e., the execution of a job can be preempted by any job of higher priority. However, tasks (jobs) do not suspend themselves before their completion. Given a set of periodic tasks and a scheduling algorithm, the response time of a job of a certain task is defined to be the time span between the request time and the completion time of the job. Liu and Layland [ 141 defined a critical instant for a task to be a time instant at which a job for that task will have the largest response time, and proved a theorem (Theorem 1 in [14]j that a critical instant for any task occurs whenever the: task is requested simultaneously with the requests of all hLgher priority tasks. A corollary of the theorem is that if a job of a certain task is requested at a critical instant of the task and the job meets its deadline, then all jobs of the task will meet their corresponding deadlines. Another corollary of the theorem is that a worst-case phasing occurs when 41 = 4 2 = . . . = &. Therefore, without loss of generality, we will assume that 4i = 0 for all i in the following discussion.

The RM algorithm assigns priorities to tasks according to their periods. Tasks with shorter periods get higher priorities. Since the periods of tasks are fixed, thl:ir priorities are also fixed.

In Section 4, we generalize our schedulability test for arbitrary task sets scheduled by any fixed-priority scheduling algorithm. In Section 5, we present some simulation results, which show that a lot of task sets that are schedulable by RM but do not satisfy Liu and Layland/Burchard's bounds can pass our schedulability test. The paper concludes with Section 6.

div.head: Simulation results
div.p: We have conducted simulations to study the improvement of our schedulability test over Liu and Lay-1and'siBurchard's utilization bounds. We present some preliminary simulation results in this section. More simulation results will be reported in a full paper.

Our simulation is conducted as follows. We randomly generate periodic task sets with total utilizations less than or equal to one but larger than Liu and Layland's/Burchard's utilization bounds, and use the necessary and sufficient condition proposed by Lehoczky et al. and Joseph and Pandya to find out those task sets that are schedulable by RM. We then apply our schedulability test (Sr and/or DCT) to these feasible task sets and check how many of them will be reported as schedulable by our schedulability test.

The simulation is run for task sets with number of tasks n from 2 up to 1000. For each task set of size n, 1000 simulation runs are performed with different random task sets and these task sets are generated with different total densities. A necessary and sufficient schedulability condition is then applied to these task sets to find out which ones are schedulable. Finally, algorithms DCT and Sr are run to check how many of the feasible task sets pass our schedulability test. We uniformly sample the total density from Burchard's utilization bound up to 0.96 with an interval 0.2 and then average the results over the sampled densities. The simulation results are depicted in Fig. 7, in which the y-axis is the percentage of the feasible task sets that pass our schedulability test.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Although a necessary and sufficient condition for a real-time periodic tiisk set to be feasibly scheduled by a fixed-priority schedtiling algorithm has been proposed, the schedulability test using this necessary and sufficient condition cannot be done in polynomial time. For the case that tasks' relative deadlines are the same as their periods, Liu and Laylarid and Burchard et al. derived closedform utilization bounds L(n) = n(2l/" -1) and B(n) = (n -1)(2ajnV1 -1) + 2l-p -1 for a task set with n tasks to be feasibly scheduled by the rate-monotonic (RM) algorithm. However, if the total utilization of a task set is larger than their bounds but less than or equal to 1, it is not known whether or not this task set is schedulable by RM.

In this paper, we proposed a polynomial-time schedulability test for periodic task sets scheduled by fixed-priority scheduling algorithms. For the case that tasks' relative deadlines are the same as their periods and the scheduling algorithm used is Rill, we proved that our schedulability test is better than using Liu and Layland'dBurchard's utilization bounds in the sense that if the total utilization of a task set is less than or equal to their bounds, our schedulability test will always answer positively for the task set, and even if a feasible task set has a total utilization larger than their bounds, our schedulability test will still answer positively with a high probability (from 100% to 83% for n = 2 to 1000). We also generalized our schedulability test to handle the general case that tasks' relative deadlines may be less than or equal to their periods and the scheduling algorithm used can be any fixed-priority scheduling algorithm. The proposed polynomial-time schedul'ability test provides a better or more efficient way for achieving predictability in designing real-time systems under fixed-priority scheduling algorithms. Moreover, we believe that this kind of nonclosed-form schedulability tests for real-time scheduling algorithms is a new direction that is worth further investigation.
